title: Judah the Prince
hook: Rabbi Judah, called simply Rabbi, gathers the oral teaching into the Mishnah

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ten martyrs, and a scroll whose letters flew up from the fire. Your line was the ten. Did you learn a name and say it? Today, a teacher makes sure the letters land somewhere safe. Day nine hundred six.

One word, with no name after it: Rabbi. That's how the Talmud can refer to Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, Judah the Prince. Just Rabbi. Nasi means prince, or leader, and he led the Jewish community of his day. But his lasting work wasn't politics. It was a book. For generations, the teachings of the sages had been passed on by mouth, teacher to student, memorized and repeated. Rabbi gathered them and set them in order. The result is called the Mishnah.
screen: `CALLED SIMPLY: RABBI.` → `NASI: THE PRINCE, THE LEADER.` → `HIS LASTING WORK: A BOOK.`

segments.voice: Here's the tension. The rabbis had a rule, recorded in the Talmud in tractate Gittin: words that were given orally, you may not say from writing. The Oral Torah was meant to live in mouths and memories, in the back and forth between a teacher and a student. Writing it down risked freezing it. So how could anyone write it down? The Talmud answers with a verse from the Psalms, read in a daring way: "It is time for the LORD to work; they have made void Thy law." The rabbis read it as: there are times when, to protect the Torah, you have to do what is normally not done. Maimonides gives Rabbi's reason this way: students were growing fewer, troubles kept coming, and teaching that lived only in memory could be lost. The tradition itself disagrees about exactly what Rabbi did. Maimonides wrote that Rabbi compiled the Mishnah and wrote it down. Rashi held that Rabbi arranged it and fixed its wording, but that it was still learned by heart, and only written later. Both agree on the heart of the matter: Rabbi gave the teaching an order. He didn't erase the arguments. The Mishnah keeps the house of Shammai beside the house of Hillel, names who said what, and records minority views. He organized without silencing. And the Talmud remembers him as a person, not only an editor: a story in tractate Bava Metzia tells that he once spared a family of small animals his maid wanted to sweep away, quoting the psalm: "His tender mercies are over all His works."
screen: `ORAL WORDS, NOT TO BE WRITTEN.` · then, large: `A TIME TO ACT FOR THE LORD.` · `MAIMONIDES AND RASHI DISAGREE.` · then: `ORDER WITHOUT SILENCING.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to organize one thing well. Sit, breathe, and pick one small thing in your life that's scattered: a pile of papers, a phone full of notes, a family recipe that lives only in one person's head. Picture what it would look like gathered and ordered, nothing important thrown out, every voice still in it. Choose the first step, small enough to do today: one folder, one page, one phone call to ask how the recipe goes. Breathe with that step until it's clear. If you pray, you can offer that work as the rabbis did their study. The bell holds the time.
Nasi. Hebrew for prince, or leader, the title carried by Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi, Judah the Prince, who gathered the sages' oral teaching into the Mishnah. Today's word.
Your line: writing it down. Today, write down one thing you know that lives only in your head, so it won't be lost. Day nine hundred six.

howItsDone: The Mishnah attributed to Rabbi Judah the Prince is the foundation text of the Talmud, studied in yeshivas, synagogues and homes, and some learners take a little each day.

what it means: Judah the Prince gathered generations of oral teaching and set it in order as the Mishnah.
what a scholar hears: the verse read as a time to act for the LORD justified writing what was meant to be oral, and Maimonides and Rashi still differ on whether Rabbi wrote it or fixed it orally.
